rule.C1.title: Consumer acknowledges automatically
rule.C1.what: A consumer on queue {queue} uses automatic acknowledgement.
rule.C1.dataSafety: No. A message is removed as soon as it is sent, so a consumer crash loses it.
rule.C1.next: Switch this consumer to manual ack, sent after the work is committed.
rule.C1.mechanism: With auto-ack the broker deletes a message the moment it writes it to the socket; whatever the consumer had not finished is gone.
rule.C2.title: Consumer prefetch is unbounded or 1
rule.C2.what: A consumer on queue {queue} has prefetch {prefetch}.
rule.C2.dataSafety: Yes. Nothing is lost; prefetch 0 can exhaust consumer memory, and prefetch 1 limits throughput.
rule.C2.next: Set prefetch on this consumer to a measured value, such as 20 to 100.
rule.C2.mechanism: Prefetch 0 lets the broker push every ready message to the consumer; prefetch 1 waits a full round trip for each message.
rule.DX1.title: Queue is used as storage
rule.DX1.what: Queue holds {ready, plural, one {# ready message} other {# ready messages}}.
rule.DX1.dataSafety: Yes. Nothing is lost yet, but a long backlog slows recovery and brings memory and disk alarms closer.
rule.DX1.next: Find out why consumers fall behind, or move long-lived data to a database.
rule.DX1.mechanism: RabbitMQ is built for short queues; with millions of ready messages, restarts, syncs and memory use grow with the backlog.
rule.DX2.title: Disk free limit is below node memory
rule.DX2.what: Node has disk_free_limit {diskFreeLimit} bytes and a memory limit of {memLimit} bytes.
rule.DX2.dataSafety: Not known. The disk can fill before the broker blocks publishers, and a full disk can lose messages.
rule.DX2.next: Set disk_free_limit to at least the memory limit of the node, for example disk_free_limit.relative = 1.0.
rule.DX2.mechanism: When paging memory to disk a node can write up to its memory size; a lower free-disk limit lets that write run out of space.
rule.DX3.title: Connections or queues are created and closed constantly
rule.DX3.what: The broker opens {connections} connections and declares {queues} queues per second.
rule.DX3.dataSafety: Yes. Nothing is lost, but the churn costs CPU and metadata writes on every node.
rule.DX3.next: Reuse long-lived connections and channels instead of opening one per request.
rule.DX3.mechanism: Each new connection and queue goes through authentication and a metadata store write; at high rates this competes with message traffic.
rule.F4.title: Messages are redelivered in a loop
rule.F4.what: Queue redelivers {redeliver} messages per second out of {deliver} delivered.
rule.F4.dataSafety: Not known. Nothing is dropped yet, but a requeue loop can hold up every other message in the queue.
rule.F4.next: Reject failing messages with requeue false so they go to dead-letter.
rule.F4.mechanism: A nack with requeue puts the message back at the head of the queue; a message that always fails is delivered again at once, without end.
rule.L3.title: Several policies match; only one applies
rule.L3.what: Policy {winner} applies; {losers} also match and are ignored.
rule.L3.dataSafety: Not known. Keys set only in the ignored policies have no effect on this object.
rule.L3.next: Merge the keys into one policy, or change the patterns so the policies do not overlap.
rule.L3.mechanism: RabbitMQ applies a single policy, the one with the highest priority, and never merges keys from other matching policies.
rule.N1.title: One connection both publishes and consumes
rule.N1.what: Connection has {publishers, plural, one {# publishing channel} other {# publishing channels}} and {consumers, plural, one {# consumer} other {# consumers}}.
rule.N1.dataSafety: Yes. Nothing is lost, but a memory alarm stalls the consumers along with the publishers.
rule.N1.next: Open separate connections for publishing and for consuming.
rule.N1.mechanism: During a resource alarm the broker blocks publishing connections; consumers on the same connection stop too, so the backlog cannot drain.
rule.N2.title: Connection has no name
rule.N2.what: A connection from user {user} sets no connection_name.
rule.N2.dataSafety: Yes. Messages are not affected; the client is only harder to identify.
rule.N2.next: Set connection_name in the client properties when opening the connection.
rule.N2.mechanism: The broker shows only an address for an unnamed connection, so tracing a finding back to a service takes guesswork.
rule.N3.title: Heartbeats are disabled
rule.N3.what: A connection from user {user} has heartbeat timeout 0.
rule.N3.dataSafety: Not known. A dead peer goes unnoticed, and its unacked messages stay held until TCP gives up.
rule.N3.next: Set a heartbeat timeout in the client, for example 60 seconds.
rule.N3.mechanism: Without heartbeats neither side notices a half-open TCP connection; its channels hold messages unacked until the operating system closes it.
rule.Q3.title: An application connects with an administrator user
rule.Q3.what: A connection uses user {user}, which is guest or has the administrator tag.
rule.Q3.dataSafety: Yes. Messages are not affected, but this application can change or delete any object.
rule.Q3.next: Create a user for this service with only the permissions it needs.
rule.Q3.mechanism: A shared administrator account lets any bug or leaked credential delete queues and policies across the broker.
rule.Q3.action: Give {objects} a service user without the administrator tag
rule.R1.title: Messages are published without confirms
rule.R1.what: A channel on connection {connection} publishes without publisher confirms.
rule.R1.dataSafety: Not known. The publisher cannot tell whether the broker took each message.
rule.R1.next: Enable publisher confirms on this channel and wait for them before treating a publish as done.
rule.R1.mechanism: Without confirms a publish returns once the bytes leave the client; a message lost in transit or on a failing node raises no error.
rule.T1.title: Durable data sits in a classic queue
rule.T1.what: This classic queue holds {messages, plural, one {# message} other {# messages}} and has {consumers, plural, one {# consumer} other {# consumers}}.
rule.T1.dataSafety: Not known. A classic queue lives on one node; if that node loses its disk, the messages are lost.
rule.T1.next: Move this queue to a quorum queue through a migration.
rule.T1.mechanism: A classic queue keeps its data on a single node with no replica; a quorum queue copies every message to a majority before confirming it.
rule.T2.title: Unroutable messages are being dropped
rule.T2.what: {count, plural, one {# unroutable message was} other {# unroutable messages were}} dropped since {since}.
rule.T2.dataSafety: No. Those messages are gone, and {exchanges} can drop more.
rule.T2.next: Set an alternate exchange on these exchanges through a policy.
rule.T2.mechanism: An exchange stores nothing: with no matching binding and no alternate exchange, the broker discards the message and still confirms it.
rule.T3.title: A full queue drops its oldest messages
rule.T3.dataSafety: No. When the queue is full, the broker deletes messages from its head to make room.
rule.T3.next: Set overflow to reject-publish or reject-publish-dlx through a policy.
rule.T3.mechanism: drop-head is the default overflow: at the length limit the broker discards the oldest message, and the publisher still gets a confirm.
rule.T4.title: Poison messages can be dropped silently
rule.T4.what: Quorum queue has no dead-letter exchange; its delivery limit is {limit}.
rule.T4.dataSafety: No. A message that reaches the delivery limit is dropped with nowhere to go; with no limit, a poison message is redelivered forever and blocks the queue.
rule.T4.next: Set a dead-letter exchange with at-least-once dead-lettering on this queue through a policy.
rule.T4.mechanism: Since 4.0 quorum queues default to a delivery limit of 20; past the limit, a message with no dead-letter target is discarded.
rule.T5.title: Dead-lettering can lose messages
rule.T5.dataSafety: No. A dead-lettered message can be lost before it reaches the parking-lot.
rule.T5.next: Set dead-letter-strategy at-least-once and overflow reject-publish together.
rule.T5.mechanism: At-least-once dead-lettering needs overflow reject-publish; without it the broker silently falls back to at-most-once.
rule.T9.title: Expired messages are deleted, not dead-lettered
rule.T9.what: Queue has {key} {value} ms and no dead-letter exchange.
rule.T9.dataSafety: No. Expired messages are deleted, and expires deletes the whole queue along with its messages.
rule.T9.next: Add a dead-letter exchange through a policy, or remove the TTL.
rule.T9.mechanism: An expired message with no dead-letter exchange is discarded; expires removes an unused queue and everything in it without dead-lettering.
rule.T9.action: Add a dead-letter exchange or remove the TTL on {objects}
rule.VT1.title: Mirrored classic queue will stop being mirrored
rule.VT1.what: Queue is mirrored by policy {policy}; mirroring is removed in {targetVersion}.
rule.VT1.dataSafety: No. After the upgrade this queue keeps one copy, and losing that node loses its messages.
rule.VT1.next: Migrate this queue to a quorum queue before upgrading.
rule.VT1.mechanism: RabbitMQ 4.0 removed classic queue mirroring; ha-mode keys are ignored and the queue silently becomes a single-node classic queue.
rule.VT1.action: Migrate {objects} to quorum queues before upgrading
rule.VT2.title: Upgrade will start dropping poison messages
rule.VT2.what: Quorum queue has no dead-letter exchange; on {targetVersion} it gets a default delivery limit of {limit}.
rule.VT2.dataSafety: No. After the upgrade, a message redelivered {limit} times is dropped.
rule.VT2.next: Set a dead-letter exchange with at-least-once dead-lettering before upgrading.
rule.VT2.mechanism: From 4.0 quorum queues have a default delivery limit; a queue that redelivered without end on 3.13 starts discarding messages instead.
rule.VT2.action: Add a dead-letter exchange to {objects} before upgrading
rule.VT3.title: Deprecated features are in use
rule.VT3.what: The broker reports these deprecated features in use: {features}.
rule.VT3.dataSafety: Yes. Nothing is lost now, but a later version can refuse or remove these features.
rule.VT3.next: Plan to stop using each listed feature before the next upgrade.
rule.VT3.mechanism: RabbitMQ marks a feature deprecated before removing it, and a broker can be set to deny it, which breaks clients that still use it.
rule.VT4.title: Nodes run different RabbitMQ versions
rule.VT4.what: Nodes in the cluster report versions {versions}.
rule.VT4.dataSafety: Yes. Mixed versions do not lose messages by themselves, but behavior can differ between nodes.
rule.VT4.next: Finish the rolling upgrade so every node runs the same version.
rule.VT4.mechanism: A cluster with mixed versions runs only the features all nodes share, and version-dependent defaults can differ from node to node.
diag.Y1.next: Remove the key or fix its spelling.
diag.Y4.message: Flow {flow} does not have exactly one target: family, queue, or exchange.
diag.Y4.next: Keep exactly one target form in this flow.
diag.Y5.message: The flow refers to family {family}, which does not exist.
diag.Y5.next: Declare family {family} or fix the name.
diag.Y6.next: Fix the template so that queue and routing_key use the same parameters.
diag.Y7.message: Family member {member} contains a reserved character: . * # / +
diag.Y7.next: Rename the member without reserved characters.
diag.Y8.message: The service refers to flow {flow}, which does not exist.
diag.Y8.next: Declare flow {flow} or fix the name.
diag.Y9.message: Waiver field {key} is missing, empty, or not a YYYY-MM-DD date.
diag.Y10.message: The waiver for {rule} expired on {until} and no longer applies.
diag.Y10.next: Renew the waiver with a later until date, or fix the finding.
diag.Y11.next: Write the object as kind and name, for example queue orders.
diag.Y12.message: ocho.yaml declares spec {spec}; this version of Ocho supports major {supported}.
diag.Y12.next: Use a version of Ocho that supports spec {spec}.
diag.Y13.message: Flow {other} already receives vhost {vhost}, exchange {exchange}, routing key {routingKey}, queue {queue}.
diag.Y13.next: Remove the overlap so that each binding belongs to one flow.
diag.Y14.next: Write broker.min_version as major.minor, for example 3.13.
diag.SNAP1.next: Take a new snapshot with this version of Ocho.
diag.SNAP2.next: Take a new snapshot instead of editing the file by hand.
diag.SNAP3.message: The snapshot breaks {count, plural, one {# model invariant} other {# model invariants}}.
diag.SNAP3.next: Attach the snapshot to an issue for the Ocho maintainers.
diag.CX1.next: Check the URL, DNS, and that the management port is open.
diag.CX2.message: The TLS certificate of {host} is invalid or not signed by a trusted CA.
diag.CX2.next: Pass the CA of the broker with --ca.
diag.CX3.message: The broker rejected user {user} at /api/overview with 401.
diag.CX3.next: Create a monitoring user: rabbitmqadmin users declare --name ocho-doctor --password-stdin --tags monitoring
diag.CX4.message: The URL contains a password, which would stay in the shell history.
diag.CX4.next: Remove the password from the URL and use password_command or --password-stdin.
diag.CX5.message: TLS verification is off because --insecure is set.
diag.CX5.next: Pass the CA of the broker with --ca and drop --insecure.
diag.CX6.message: Context file {file} has mode {mode}, wider than 0600.
diag.CX6.next: Run chmod 600 on the context file.
diag.CX7.message: password_command failed or ran longer than {seconds} seconds.
diag.CX7.next: Run the password_command by hand and fix its output.
diag.CX8.message: RabbitMQ {version} is older than {min}, the oldest version Ocho supports.
diag.CX8.next: Upgrade the broker to {min} or later.
diag.OC1.message: A read-only command runs as {user}, which has the administrator tag.
diag.OC1.next: Create a user with only the monitoring tag for Ocho.
reason.forbidden.unlock: Give the monitoring tag to the user Ocho connects with
reason.endpoint_missing: this broker version has no {path} endpoint
reason.model_mismatch: Ocho computed a different effective policy than the broker
reason.model_mismatch.unlock: Send a snapshot taken with --save --redact-hosts in an issue
reason.tie: policies {policies} match with the same priority
reason.tie.unlock: Give one of these policies a higher priority
reason.regex_unsupported: policy {policy} uses a pattern Ocho cannot match exactly
reason.regex_unsupported.unlock: Rewrite the pattern without atomic groups, possessive quantifiers, \Z or inline flags
reason.inconsistent_read: objects changed while Ocho was reading them
reason.depends_on: it depends on {path}, which is unknown
exclusion.EX1: The default exchange cannot be configured.
exclusion.EX2: The amq. prefix is reserved; the broker creates these exchanges itself.
exclusion.EX3: This amq. exchange has no outgoing binding, so it carries no flow.
exclusion.EX4: An exclusive queue belongs to one connection and is temporary.
exclusion.EX5: The broker generated this queue name.
exclusion.EX6: MQTT subscription queues belong to rules T11 and T12, outside Ocho v0.1.
exclusion.EX7: Ocho manages its own system objects; they get their own rules later.
exclusion.EX8: This is an implicit binding of the default exchange.
exclusion.EX9: Direct reply-to requires automatic acknowledgement, so this is not a C1 finding.
